name: Rafael Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my dad's farm, 70 hectares on the Kestrel Road, and I've run it since he died six years ago. Forty suckler cows, winter wheat and a lot of hay. In summer I bale for half the neighbours with an old Welger baler, which is where the spare cash comes from. In winter it's feeding, bedding and mending gates that the bulls lean on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is being my own boss on land my family's had for three generations. Hard is the loan: I borrowed to buy out my sister's share when Dad died, so the farm has a mortgage it never had before. My wife Nadia works on the front desk at the vet practice in town, and her wage is the steady one. We've less than a month saved. I don't use any of this AI stuff; my phone still has buttons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, at the mart, probably over a bacon roll. Most of it was always talk. I don't go online much, so that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes, and that's not good news either. Beef prices were down again this autumn and the loan payment doesn't care. I'm farming to pay the bank, and the plateau doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the suckler herd at forty and push for more baling customers next summer. I'd sell the old quad bike and use the tractor for checking stock. We'd cancel the satellite TV, because the kids watch everything on their phones anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, a bit worn down. You get used to the weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm loan payment in February, because it lands right when there's no money coming in. Calves don't sell till autumn. Last year I sold six bales of hay to a horse lady just to cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Nadia talk about at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly whether Sami needs new football boots again. Nadia does the household sums; I do the farm sums. We try not to put them side by side too often.

say: Most of the AI talk was **always just talk**.
I'd say it over a bacon roll at the **mart**, not online.
think: Nothing changes, and **beef prices** were already down this autumn.
I'm farming **to pay the bank**, and that stays the same.
do: Keep the herd at **forty cows** and find more baling customers.
Sell the **old quad bike** and check stock by tractor.
feel: **Worn down**, used to carrying the same weight.
S0.quote: I'm farming to pay the bank, and the plateau doesn't change that.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **buy-out loan** taken when his father died.
**Nadia's wage** is the steady income that props up the farm.
He separates **household and farm sums** to avoid facing them together.

steps.text: Keep the herd at forty suckler cows
Sell the old quad bike and cancel satellite TV
Sign up three more neighbours for summer hay baling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for me, cows don't care about computers. I'd probably joke at the mart that the office folk are getting a taste of farming luck. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits Nadia, not me. Cows don't care about computers, but my wife answers phones for a living. Her whole job is booking appointments and answering the phone at the vet's, and that's exactly what the card says goes. If her hours get cut, we lose the steady money that pays the mortgage while the farm pays the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the vet practice actually does before panicking. If Nadia's hours went down, I'd ask her parents to have the kids after school so she could pick up shifts elsewhere. I'd also cut the farm spending: no new fencing, patch what we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for myself, worried sick for Nadia. I'd hide that from her, probably badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the vet practice said anything yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia says they've already got an online booking page that half the clients ignore. The new manager talks about a phone system that answers itself. Nadia laughs about it, but she's checked the job ads twice this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What other work is there near you if Nadia needed it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much: the supermarket in town, a care home, the school kitchen. She's good with people, so she'd find something. It just wouldn't pay what the vet's does.

say: It's fine for me, because **cows don't care** about computers.
The office folk are getting a taste of **farming luck**.
think: Steady Disruption hits **Nadia's front-desk job**, not my farm work.
Losing her hours means losing the **steady money** for the mortgage.
do: **Wait and see** what the vet practice actually does.
Ask **Nadia's parents** to mind the kids if she needs new shifts.
Stop new fencing and **patch the old** instead.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself but **worried sick** for Nadia, and hiding it.
S1.quote: Cows don't care about computers, but my wife answers phones for a living.
fieldNote: The real exposure in his household is **Nadia's booking job**.
His public joke and private fear show a clear **say–think gap**.
His instinct is to **wait**, then lean on family.

steps.text: Wait to see if the vet practice cuts Nadia's hours
Ask Nadia's parents to mind Sami and Lina after school
Patch old fences instead of buying new fencing this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone in charge should have seen it coming. I'd say it at the mart and at the school gate. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign a petition. Families like ours need help fast when it hits before anyone is ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 2028 takes Nadia's job outright, I'm sure of it. Then around 2031 the neighbours buy robot balers or hire a robot contractor, and my baling money goes too. The cows might last a bit longer. The farm on its own has never paid the loan, and robots would take the baling money that does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year after Nadia's job went, I'd rent the wheat ground to the big Pemberton farm next door and keep only the cattle. I'd sell the old baler while it's still worth something. And we'd go to the bank to stretch the loan before we start missing payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can feel it in my chest just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Sami and Lina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell my kids much, honestly, just that we're tightening up for a while. Sami would guess anyway, he's thirteen. Lina would ask if we can still keep the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new technology. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have no choice, would I? If the bank wants everything online, I'd make Nadia do it, or Sami. I'm not proud of that.

say: Somebody in charge **should have seen it** coming.
I'm not one for marches, but I'd **sign a petition**.
Families like ours need **help fast** when it hits before anyone is ready.
think: Robots by 2031 take my **baling money**, and the farm alone can't pay the loan.
do: Rent the **wheat ground** to the big Pemberton farm.
Sell the **old baler** while it's worth something.
Ask the bank to **stretch the loan** before missing payments.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling it physically in his chest.
S2.quote: The farm on its own has never paid the loan, and robots would take the baling money that does.
fieldNote: He maps both hits clearly: **Nadia in 2028**, his baling in 2031.
His exit is **renting land**, not selling the family farm.
He'd lean on **his wife and son** for anything online.

steps.text: Rent the wheat fields to the Pemberton farm next door
Sell the old Welger baler before prices drop
Cut the household to essentials while Nadia looks for work
Ask the bank to stretch the farm loan repayments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people stop arguing and plan. I'd say farmers should get help to adjust. That's about all I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the same story as the fast one, but Nadia's got until 2031 and I keep baling till about 2034. That's long enough to pay a good chunk off the loan. I'd still lose the baling in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nadia to look for a different job now, maybe the care home or the school, before the vet's goes. I'd put every baling payment above the loan instalment into overpaying the loan. I'd hold off renting the land for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could plan. Five years is like seeing the bull coming across the field: you've time to get to the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Nadia want to switch jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she loves the animals and the clients. It'd be a hard talk, and she'd say I'm panicking about nothing. Maybe I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I should learn how these robot balers work, so I could rent one and keep the customers. I don't fancy it. But I'd rather do that than lose the neighbours.

say: Five years is enough if people **stop arguing** and plan.
Farmers should get **help to adjust** to the change.
think: Nadia has until **2031** and I keep baling till about 2034.
That's long enough to **pay down** a good chunk of the loan.
do: Ask Nadia to look for a **new job** before the vet's goes.
Overpay the **farm loan** with baling money.
Hold off **renting out** the land for now.
feel: **Anxious**, but with **time to plan**, like having time to reach the gate.
S3.quote: Five years is like seeing the bull coming across the field: you've time to get to the gate.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **pay down debt** instead of selling.
Pushing Nadia to switch jobs early may **cause friction** at home.
He grudgingly considers **renting a robot baler** to keep customers.

steps.text: Overpay the farm loan with every spare baling payment
Help Nadia apply for jobs at the care home or school
Hold off renting out the wheat fields until 2033

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, plenty of time, let's not lose our heads. I'd say it at the mart. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means the loan could be nearly paid by the time the robots come in 2039. I'd be 56, Sami and Lina would be grown. Nadia's job still goes earlier, around 2036, but by then the kids are out of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming the way I do. I'd overpay the loan when I could. I'd make sure the kids know the farm is theirs if they want it, but not to count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the old worry. Same weight, but I can carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Sami and Lina to do with their lives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything that keeps them near home, if I'm honest. My dad wanted me to stay on the farm and I did, but I wouldn't put that on my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if beef prices fall further in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd cut the herd to thirty and grow more hay. The baling would keep us afloat. It always has.

say: Plenty of time, so **let's not lose** our heads.
Nobody round here should **panic** about something that is ten years off.
think: The loan could be **nearly paid** by the time robots come in 2039.
Nadia's job goes around **2036**, when the kids are grown.
do: Tell the kids the farm is **theirs if they want** it.
S4.quote: My dad wanted me to stay on the farm and I did, but I wouldn't put that on my kids.
fieldNote: The decade lets his **loan run down** before the robots.
His bottom line is still **beef prices** and the loan.
He won't press his kids to **inherit the farm**.

steps.text: Keep running forty suckler cows and summer baling
Overpay the buy-out loan in good baling years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because Nadia's job goes first and then my baling, and the farm can't carry the loan alone. What would help is the bank giving farmers time, a payment holiday or longer terms. And some help for Nadia to retrain without losing her wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. My dad knew every hedge on this farm by name. A robot will cut a hedge, but it won't know my dad planted it.

headlineQuote: A robot will cut a hedge, but it won't know my dad planted it.
portrait: Rafael, 43, runs his late father's **70-hectare** beef and wheat farm with a buy-out loan.
Summer **hay baling** for neighbours brings in the spare cash, and he never uses AI tools.
His wife Nadia's **vet front-desk job** is the steady wage and the most exposed one.
He waits, cuts back and leans on family; in the fast world he'd **rent out land**.
He's **anxious** in most worlds and **alarmed** when both incomes go before the loan is paid.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Nadia's job and then his baling would go before the loan is paid.
whatWouldHelp: **Longer bank terms** for farmers, and paid retraining for Nadia.
